doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Audiences, rock and roll and Elvis
summary: Fraternity crowds loved the music, rock and roll came after college, and a view on Elvis as watershed.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: And the people you played for, did you ever have some of the frat fellas like, “Play some rock & roll?”

Not in those days. They loved the stuff. And that’s I think the sad part of the world for me today is that the audience is going away. It was so much fun. I mean you’d go in and you’d have just throngs of people. You know on a nice spring evening you’d wind up on some terrace you know and half the Cornell football team would carry the grand piano out on the terrace and it would be a nice night and there’d be all sorts of people. They loved the music and it was so much fun. But that’s what the music was. Rock & roll really hadn’t — we were just a little before that, really Elvis got going while we were — really after we were out of college.

Okay. Yeah because that was a sort of a — I don’t know if I would call it a down time for pop music but there wasn’t anything really strong for a number of years there so I think your timing was pretty good for that.

Some people who are historians and know about this stuff really think that Elvis was a watershed. And some very fine musicians believe that, you know, he wasn’t just a kind of a great pop guy, I mean he really made a huge difference in how we all thought about and listened to music. Leonard Bernstein said that.
